summary: Lunar Exploration is a free 3D browser game that lets school-age players walk a tiny Moon and Mars and meet 15 machines NASA left behind, each placed where it really landed. Walk up to Eagle's descent stage, a lunar rover or Ingenuity, scan it, and the machine tells its own story in first person. Its card then flips to a "then and now" slider: an archival NASA photo against a Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter or HiRISE image of the same site today. Hands-on experiments show how the hardware made science possible: time a laser pulse to the Apollo 11 retroreflector, or crash a spent Apollo stage and watch the Moon ring for nearly an hour. Every fact is cited to NASA sources. A Field Trip button gives teachers a room code so a whole class can explore together, live, in any browser. The story ends by asking what Artemis will leave behind.
details:
What it does

Lunar Exploration is a story-driven 3D exploration game that runs in any desktop or phone browser, with no install or login. You play an astronaut on a tiny walkable Moon. CAPCOM radios you missions, and 15 pieces of hardware NASA left on the Moon and Mars wait at their real landing sites (shrunk onto a small planet, with the real latitude and longitude shown on the map):

  • The Scouts: Ranger 7, Surveyor 3
  • The Footprints: Apollo 11's Eagle descent stage and Laser Ranging Retroreflector, the Apollo 12 Passive Seismic Experiment, the Apollo 15 and 17 Lunar Roving Vehicles, Apollo 17's Challenger
  • Crashing on Purpose: Apollo 16's Orion, LCROSS, GRAIL's twins Ebb and Flow
  • The Red Planet: after a rocket flight, Viking 1, Sojourner, Opportunity and Ingenuity on a walkable Mars
  • What We Leave Behind: an ending on space-heritage protection and what Artemis will leave next

When you scan a machine, it speaks in first person ("I'm Eagle's descent stage..."), so players meet each one as a character, not a list of facts. Its trading card flips to a "then and now" slider that wipes between an archival NASA photo and a Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, HiRISE or Perseverance image of the same spot today. A kid on Earth, KID-1, radios the questions a young player would ask ("Why did they leave it there?").

How hardware made science possible: two experiments. At the retroreflector you fire a laser from an Earth observatory, watch the ~2.5 s round trip and see the distance computed (d = c·t/2); it is still used today and shows the Moon drifting away about 3.8 cm a year. At the Apollo 12 seismometer you crash the spent ascent stage and watch the seismograph ring for about 55 minutes (sped up), the result that showed the Moon's crust is dry and fractured.

Classroom field trip. A teacher presses Field Trip, reads out a short room code, and the whole class walks the same Moon live, with name tags (filtered for safe callsigns) and emotes.

How we built it

TypeScript, React 19 and three.js through React Three Fiber and drei; zustand for state; Trystero for peer-to-peer WebRTC multiplayer (no game server), with a Cloudflare Worker for TURN credentials when networks block direct connections; Vite to build; Cloudflare Pages to host, deployed by GitHub Actions. Four official NASA 3D models (Apollo Lunar Module, Viking Lander, Opportunity, Ingenuity) were shrunk with glTF Transform from about 4.5 MB to under 1 MB and given a shared cel-shading ramp; the rocket, astronaut and other hardware are built in code. Every sound is synthesised with Web Audio. Unit tests cover missions, saves, experiments, flight, geo maths and terrain.

Benefits and intended impact

The challenge asks for a personal connection to forgotten robotic explorers. Letting each machine speak, and then showing its real site from orbit decades later, turns "a lander on the Moon" into "Eagle, still sitting where Armstrong left it." It is free, loads in seconds on a school laptop or phone, needs no accounts, and a class can play together, so a teacher can use it in a single lesson.

What's creative

Hardware as narrator; a tiny-planet museum where the map still tells the truth (real coordinates); then/now orbital photos as a game reward; experiments with no fail state; and the story ordered as acts, so walking the Moon also walks through time, from Ranger in 1964 to Ingenuity in 2024.

What we considered

Accuracy first: all 15 cards were fact-checked and cite NASA sources on the card and in the end credits. Where no camera can see a site (Cabeus crater's floor is in permanent shadow) we use the LRO laser-altimeter map and say so; GRAIL's "then" image is NASA artwork and is labelled as art. Short sentences for ages 9 to 14. Keyboard, mouse and touch controls, reduced-motion support, and a total download of a few MB. We use no NASA logos or insignia as our branding; the rocket carries our own patch.

What existed before the event

Our repository was created on Nov 6, 2026 with an empty commit. The first code, design doc and assets landed on Nov 8, and most of the game (3D prototype, multiplayer, story data, physics) was built Nov 8-13, before the Nov 14-15 hackathon weekend. Terrain, textures, the rocket redesign and final polish were done on Nov 14. An early 2D concept was replaced by this 3D game on Nov 8. The event rules allow work started before the hackathon weekend; the git history is the full record.
